# Your first project {#your-first-project}

::: {.doc-lead}
Bring a plot into a figure. Give it a caption, a place in your manuscript, and a moment in your presentation. The same work stays connected throughout.
:::

<div class="guide-meta"><span>About 20 minutes</span><span>All five workspaces</span><span>Beginner</span></div>

You'll need [Flux installed](/install/). The plotting step uses Python and fluxplot; you can also begin with an SVG or PNG you already have. All numbers in the small example below are **synthetic**.

Shortcuts are written with **Ctrl** and **Alt**. On macOS, press **⌘ Command** for Ctrl and **⌥ Option** for Alt; [Keyboard shortcuts](/docs/shortcuts.html) lists them all.

## 1. Give the work a home {#create}

Create a working folder called `growth-study`. In Flux, choose **New project** from Home and create a project named `paper` inside that folder.

```text
growth-study/
└── paper/         ← your Flux project
```

Your analysis code will live in `growth-study`; the project holds the writing, plots, figures, references, and slides. Flux autosaves your work, so you will not press Save again in this walkthrough. If saving reports an error, resolve it before closing the app.

You can return to the project from Home, or open it from a terminal:

```bash
flux /path/to/growth-study/paper
```

**You now have** an empty project folder of ordinary files. [Learn how projects and files fit together](projects-and-files.qmd).

## 2. Make a plot with named parts {#plot}

In a terminal, move to `growth-study` and create a Python environment:

```bash
uv init
uv add fluxplot
```

Save the following as `make_growth.py` beside the `paper` folder. You use ordinary matplotlib axes; fluxplot adds a stable name to each series and saves the semantic files.

```python
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import fluxplot as fp

time = [0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24]
control = [0.02, 0.05, 0.13, 0.41,
           0.95, 1.60, 1.90]
treatment = [0.02, 0.07, 0.25, 0.80,
             1.50, 1.95, 2.10]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 3.2))
fp.line(ax, time, control,
        series="control",
        marker="o", label="Control")
fp.line(ax, time, treatment,
        series="treatment",
        marker="s", label="Treatment")
ax.set(xlabel="Time (h)",
       ylabel="Illustrative response")
ax.set_title("Synthetic growth profiles")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()

here = Path(__file__).resolve()
plots = here.parent / "paper" / "plots"
plots.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
recipe = {"script": str(here),
          "params": {}, "inputs": []}
fp.save(fig, plots / "growth.svg",
        recipe=recipe)
```

Run it:

```bash
uv run python make_growth.py
```

**You now have** three neighbouring files in `paper/plots/`: `growth.svg`, `growth.fluxplot.json`, and `growth.recipe.json`. Keep them together. The SVG is the visible plot; the manifest describes its parts and data; the recipe records its producing script. The two `series=` names, `control` and `treatment`, are the handles everything downstream uses.

::: {.doc-note}
**Already have a plot?** Import any SVG or PNG to continue. Per-part editing and data morphs require semantic information, which fluxplot records when it creates a plot.
:::

## 3. Compose and refine in Figure {#figure}

1. Switch to **Figure** in the title bar (or **Ctrl+1**) and press **Alt+G**. The sidebar switches to its **Plots** view and lists `growth.svg`, marked **◆**: an editable fluxplot.
2. **Double-click** the plot, or drag it onto the figure. It lands at its true printed size, 4.8 × 3.2 inches, exactly as Python saved it.

   <figure class="doc-figure doc-clip"><video poster="/assets/media/docs/clips/plots-rail-place.png" width="1400" height="1000" muted loop playsinline autoplay controls preload="metadata" aria-label="The tutorial plot is dragged from the sidebar’s Plots view onto an empty figure and lands at its printed size."><source src="/assets/media/docs/clips/plots-rail-place.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video><figcaption>Drag <code>growth.svg</code> from the Plots view onto the figure. It lands at 4.8 × 3.2 inches, exactly as Python saved it.</figcaption></figure>

3. **Ctrl+click** the control line. You have selected one *part* of the plot, not the whole picture. Press **F** to open its property menu and change the stroke colour. The restyle is keyed to the series name `control`, so it survives when the plot is regenerated.


4. Press **R** to open the **X-ray**: the plot's anatomy as a tree beside the selection. Hovering a row outlines that part on the canvas; **x** hides a part; **Regenerate** re-runs the recipe from inside the panel. **Escape** closes it.

   <figure class="doc-figure doc-clip"><video poster="/assets/media/docs/clips/xray.png" width="1400" height="1000" muted loop playsinline autoplay controls preload="metadata" aria-label="Ctrl+click selects the control series line; pressing R opens the X-ray panel beside the plot, a tree of its parts; moving over rows outlines those parts on the canvas."><source src="/assets/media/docs/clips/xray.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video><figcaption><strong>Ctrl+click</strong> a part, press <strong>R</strong>: the X-ray lists the plot’s anatomy, and hovering a row lights that part on the canvas.</figcaption></figure>

5. Change a number in `make_growth.py` and run it again. Flux refreshes the linked plot in place and keeps the colour you chose. Resize the plot by dragging an edge or corner if you like: a fluxplot ≥ 0.4 plot **reflows**, so its text, strokes and markers keep their point size while the axes grow or shrink.
6. Press **Alt+M** to open **Figure-Meta** and write the caption. For this example: "Synthetic growth profiles for two illustrative conditions. Points show constructed values at seven time points; lines connect successive observations."

**You now have** a figure with a linked, restyled plot and a caption. The figure catalogue shows whether the link is current, missing, or needs attention. [Figure](/docs/figure.html) · [Editing plots](/docs/plot-editing.html#x-ray) · [Figure shortcuts](/docs/shortcuts.html#figure)

## 4. Collect and read a reference {#read}

1. Open **Library** (**Ctrl+4**) and paste a paper's DOI into the add box, then press **Enter**. The reference joins your shared library, where it is available across projects. (**Import…** reads a BibTeX or RIS file instead.)
2. Press **Enrich** to fill in the abstract, topics and citation counts, and the row's **⬇** to fetch an open-access PDF when one exists.
3. Click the row once: that copies its citation key, which you will paste into the manuscript in step 5.
4. **Ctrl+Shift+click** the row to open the paper in **Reader**. Select a sentence and choose a highlight colour, then click the highlight to attach a note. Highlights anchor to the text itself and stay with the paper.

**You now have** a reference you can cite and a paper you have read and marked up. Reader also supports tabs, side-by-side reading, and figure snips that retain their source provenance. A reference in your Library becomes part of a project's bibliography when you cite it; [Library and project references](projects-and-files.qmd#library) explains the distinction.

## 5. Write with the figure in view {#write}

Switch to **Paper** (**Ctrl+2**) and write a short paragraph. Three insertions connect the document to your work:

- Type **`/figure`** and choose your figure to embed it with its caption. (**Alt+F** opens the Figures pane, which can also insert the figure or a reference to it or one of its panels.)
- Type **`@@`** to insert a cross-reference to the figure in your prose; the number maintains itself.
- Type **`@`** and the first author's name to choose the citation from your library. Pasting a DOI straight into the text works too.

Figure numbering follows the designation you choose in Figure. Reordering paragraphs does not renumber your figures. The permanent reference stays attached when you rename a figure or move it between canvases.

**You now have** a manuscript that refers to your figure and your reference. It remains a `.qmd` file: you can write equations, add tables, keep working notes, and review comments alongside the prose.

## 6. Let the explanation unfold {#present}

1. Back in **Figure**, select the figure and choose **Send to deck…** in the Inspector. Flux copies the figure onto a new slide at its native size.
2. Open **Slides** (**Ctrl+3**) and press **Animate ⏱** to open the animator. Select the plot and click **✨ Auto-animate**: Flux builds the plot's entrance from its own anatomy in three clicks — **Axes & grid**, then **Data** (the lines draw on), then **Legend & annotations**.
3. Press **F5** to present. Advance with **→** or **Space**; **Back** plays the step you just saw in reverse. **Escape** leaves.
4. **Export** produces a single `.html` file that plays the talk in any browser, offline.

**You now have** a slide built from the same plot source as your figure. Add a step for the next part of your explanation, then use the animation tools to reveal an element or transform it into a later state.

An interactive slide can also live inside a Paper document. HTML preserves its steps; PDF and Word use a still. The example below runs in Flux's native player. These are the slides from the Flux film, made from plots in the demonstration project.

```{=html}
<div class="slide-demo" id="slide-demo" data-demo-src="/demos/slides/index.html" data-demo-scene="2">
<button type="button" class="demo-launch" aria-label="Load the interactive slides from the Flux film" data-demo-start><img src="/demos/studies/become.svg" alt="A slide titled “In Flux, any figure can become a slide”: the dots of the Flux mark have become five coloured shapes. Load the native slides to play them." width="1280" height="720" loading="lazy"><span class="demo-launch-prompt"><span class="play-disc" aria-hidden="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="m9 6 9 6-9 6Z" /></svg></span><span>Play the slides<small>The slides from the film, running in your browser</small></span></span></button>
```

The example opens on the slide made live in the film: the dots of a plotted Flux mark become five shapes and a caption. Use the arrows to advance, or choose another slide from the menu. Each slide names its data source below the player. [Visual credits](/docs/visual-credits.html#slides) · [Slides guide](/docs/slides.html).

## 7. Export and keep the sources {#export}

In Paper, choose **Export** and select PDF. Flux's built-in PDF export does not require Quarto. Word export uses Quarto; install it through **Set up Flux** if needed, and tick **Live Zotero citations** if a co-author will edit the citations in Word. The command-line route, `flux compile --to pdf`, uses Quarto and also needs TeX ([PDF dependencies](/docs/export-documents.html#pdf-dependencies)).

Check the exported figures, captions, and references, then keep your project folder alongside the result. It contains the editable work you will want for the next revision.

**You have now seen the loop**: read → plot → compose → write → cite → export, all in one folder. From here, the workspace guides go deeper, and when the study grows, [regenerate plots instead of re-saving them](/docs/semantic-plots.html#regenerate-dont-re-save). When you are ready for a collaborator who composes and cites *for* you, [connect an agent](/docs/connect.html).
